bivy.name: Glacier Basin
bivy.water: Running creek water in the basin — the last easy water before the glaciers, and the reason most parties top off here rather than carrying from the trailhead.
bivy.capacity: Five individual backcountry sites plus one group site.
bivy.permit: A National Park Service wilderness permit is required for any overnight stay in Mount Rainier's backcountry; roughly two thirds of summer sites are reservable on Recreation.gov and the remainder are issued first-come at a ranger station.
bivy.notes: The last forested camp on the route, in the valley below Mount Ruth and Burroughs Mountain, about 3.5 mi up the Glacier Basin Trail from White River Campground. There is a composting toilet a short walk from the sites and screw-top bear barrels for food. Parties who cannot get a Camp Schurman permit, or who want to break the climb into three days, sleep here and take the Inter Glacier the following morning.

bivy.name: Camp Schurman
bivy.water: None running. Everything is melted from snow, so budget fuel accordingly.
bivy.capacity: Around 50 people a night — the second-busiest climbing camp on the mountain after Camp Muir.
bivy.permit: Overnight stays require a wilderness permit, and a separate climbing permit covers travel above 10,000 ft or on glaciers.
bivy.notes: Sits on the rock of Steamboat Prow where the Emmons and Winthrop glaciers part. There is a ranger hut with an emergency radio mounted on the outside that reaches dispatch when no ranger is in residence, and a single solar-dehydrating outhouse. That toilet is closed up from October through May, so off-season parties carry blue bags; early-season parties have also found the whole facility still buried in snow well into May. Nothing is hauled out for you — all rubbish goes back down in your pack.

bivy.name: Emmons Flats
bivy.capacity: A handful of tents; used as overflow and by parties wanting a slightly shorter summit day.
bivy.permit: Camping here is granted by the rangers rather than assumed — ask at Camp Schurman.
bivy.notes: A bench a tenth or two of a mile up and over the hill from Camp Schurman, five minutes' walk in good conditions. Several large crevasses lie between the two camps, bridged in early season and not always later, so move between them roped as a team rather than walking over unroped with a water bottle.

bivy.name: Curtis Ridge
bivy.capacity: Several flat spots — noticeably more room than Thumb Rock, which is why parties expecting company start here.
bivy.permit: Mount Rainier National Park wilderness permit for the night plus a climbing permit for the glacier travel above; walk-up registration is at the White River Wilderness Information Center.
bivy.notes: The standard first night, on the broad snow shoulder near the gully used to drop onto the Carbon Glacier, reached over St. Elmo Pass and across the lower Winthrop. Flat ground and comparatively little rockfall exposure. It is not free of hazard: a party camped here watched a large avalanche off the Willis Wall push its debris cloud close to the bivy. Because Thumb Rock is cramped, leaving here early is the difference between a site and no site.

bivy.name: Thumb Rock
bivy.capacity: Only a few tents. Sites are small and often staggered a few feet apart vertically down the slope rather than side by side.
bivy.notes: The one real camp on the ridge itself, in the saddle just above the rock feature, reached by 45-55 degree snow and ice. Published elevations for it disagree — reports place it anywhere from about 10,400 to 10,800 ft. It is exposed to rock and ice coming off the Thumb and off the bands higher up, and that exposure has killed people here, so parties build up or repair the rock walls around the platforms. Strong teams in good conditions skip it entirely, camping at Curtis Ridge and climbing the ridge in a single push to cut the hours spent under the fall line.

bivy.name: Hogsback
bivy.water: Meltwater streams run at camp — this is the last running water, and there is none once you are on the Coleman. Treat it; nothing here is potable as found. Flow swings hard with the sun, so a channel that is a step across at dawn can be a torrent by mid-afternoon.
bivy.capacity: Sites are scattered along roughly 200 ft of moraine crest between 6,000 and 6,200 ft, so exactly where you end up depends on water and on who got there first. It is a busy camp — several parties most summer weekends.
bivy.permit: No quota or overnight permit; a valid Recreation Pass must be displayed at the Heliotrope Ridge trailhead (a Washington Sno-Park permit for winter parking on Glacier Creek Road). Mount Baker Wilderness rules apply: parties of 12 or fewer, no campfires of any kind, self-contained stoves only.
bivy.notes: Shared with the Coleman-Deming route and reached by branching off Trail 677 at the old Kulshan Cabin site and climbing the moraine crest. There are no trees at this elevation, so food has to go in a bear canister or Ursack — the nearest suitable trees for hanging are lower, at Harrison Camp. Human waste goes out in blue bags; burial is not permitted on snow, rock or alpine ground. From here the North Ridge parts company with Coleman-Deming: rope up, cross the Coleman climbers' right below the Colfax icefall, and gain the ridge on the glacier's true right.

bivy.name: The Lunch Counter
bivy.water: Unreliable. When nights stay above freezing there is meltwater at the foot of the snowfield between Suksdorf Ridge and the Mazama Glacier, but it is occasional even in midsummer and gone once the snow pulls back. Plan on melting snow or carrying up what you need.
bivy.capacity: Large and informal — a spread of bare bench with dozens of stone windbreaks that climbers have built and rebuilt over the years. Room for many parties, and on summer weekends there are many.
bivy.permit: A Mt. Adams Climbing Pass is required from 1 May to 30 September for anyone 16 or older going above 7,000 ft, whether or not they intend to summit; it is bought on Recreation.gov and must be carried on you and shown in the vehicle windscreen. From October through April a self-issued wilderness permit replaces it. Human waste must be packed out in carry-out bags (free at the Mt. Adams Ranger District) because decomposition above 7,000 ft is too slow to keep up. Group size limit is 12; no campfires.
bivy.notes: The standard high camp, a broad rubble-and-snow bench up the South Spur above the Crescent Glacier; sources put it anywhere from about 9,000 to 9,400 ft depending which shelf you stop on. Wind is the defining problem — pitch inside an existing rock wall and expect to rebuild part of it. Being above treeline it is a bad place to be caught in a thunderstorm, which on Adams typically builds in the afternoon. Summit day from here is commonly 4-5 hours up.

bivy.name: Morrison Creek drainage
bivy.water: Morrison Creek is the last dependable running water on the approach and a common place to top off.
bivy.permit: Below 7,000 ft only a free self-issued wilderness permit is needed, so a camp here sits outside the climbing-pass requirement.
bivy.notes: Lower option below the Crescent Glacier, used by parties who would rather not sleep in the crowds and wind at the Lunch Counter. It costs you elevation on summit day. Morrison Creek Campground further down the road is also used by parties arriving late who do not want to drive the rough final miles of FR 8040 in the dark.

bivy.name: Valley bivy below the buttress
bivy.water: Running water in the drainage below the buttress; the approach itself crosses Grizzly Creek, which is the last easy fill before the brush.
bivy.capacity: A small site — a party or two on sparse timber and rock benches near the toe of the buttress.
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit. A cross-country zone permit covers one party for one night in that zone; most zones cap a party at six people, camping is restricted to snow, rock or bare ground, fires are prohibited, and waste is buried or carried out in blue bags above treeline.
bivy.notes: The classic first night, and it is earned: parties commonly take about eight hours from the trailhead, down the PCT to the North Fork Bridge Creek trail, then up past Grizzly Creek into slabs, brush and talus. The usual log over Grizzly Creek has broken and a replacement has been found roughly 200 ft south of the trail; the trail beyond that crossing is badly overgrown. Reports place sites in sparse timber around 5,200 ft and on rock benches east of the buttress toe nearer 5,600 ft.

bivy.name: Goode Glacier moraine
bivy.water: Meltwater — parties describe waterfalls running beside the moraine camp.
bivy.capacity: A couple of tents on the moraine crest and meadow benches.
bivy.notes: The higher option, on the lateral moraine looking across at the seracs of the Goode Glacier, variously reported between about 6,400 and 7,000 ft. It shortens the climbing day considerably over the valley bivy and puts you in wildflower meadow with a view, at the cost of carrying the load higher on approach day.

bivy.name: Summit bivy
bivy.water: None on top. The nearest is a large snow patch a few hundred feet down at the saddle northwest of the summit, which has to be fetched and melted.
bivy.capacity: Room for about three — a fourth party member or a second rope team has to drop off and find something else.
bivy.notes: Parties who start from the valley often finish the buttress too late to descend and sleep on the summit itself. There is also a grassy ledge reported around 8,500 ft on the upper route that one party found softer and more comfortable than the top. Both are dry, exposed perches, so they only work in settled weather.

bivy.name: Colonial Basin
bivy.capacity: Five or six sites, most of them ringed with rock wind walls.
bivy.permit: Backcountry permit from the North Cascades complex — parties pick these up at the Marblemount ranger station or reserve through Recreation.gov. Cross-country zone permits cover one party per night, camping is on snow, rock or bare ground only and never in meadow or within 100 ft of water, and fires are prohibited.
bivy.notes: Reached by the steep, narrow climbers' path above Pyramid Lake; you break out of trees near 5,600 ft and the basin opens below Colonial and Pyramid. It is a spectacular spot and a genuinely windy one — parties have needed several people and a pile of rocks to get a tent up. A few sites tucked into alcoves shelter far better than the open ground, so look before you pitch.

bivy.name: Colonial-Neve col
bivy.water: A stream and a small waterfall at the col, plus tarns nearby.
bivy.capacity: Two or three sites, with wind walls already built.
bivy.notes: The high camp, on the col between the Colonial and Neve glaciers, and the one most parties push to if they have the legs. Dry ground, better sheltered than the basin below, and it puts the Neve Glacier and the west ridge within a short morning. Getting here involves glacier travel, so it is a rope-up-before-camp proposition rather than a walk.

bivy.name: Lower camp below the basin
bivy.water: Snowmelt and seasonal runoff; Pyramid Lake at 2,600 ft is the last certain water low on the approach.
bivy.notes: The bail-out option around 5,400 ft, just below where the climbers' path leaves the trees, used by parties who run out of daylight or energy on the steep section above Pyramid Lake. It leaves a long second day to the summit and back.

bivy.name: Colchuck Lake
bivy.water: The lake, which is often still part-frozen in the season this route is in condition.
bivy.capacity: Numerous sites strung along the shoreline and more clustered at the north end. Under the overnight quota the Colchuck zone issues a small number of permits a day, group permits included, so the camp is never as crowded as the day-hiker traffic suggests.
bivy.permit: An Enchantment Permit Area overnight permit is required from 15 May to 31 October and must be obtained in advance through Recreation.gov, with the advance lottery running mid-February to 1 March. Group size is capped at eight, campfires are prohibited, dogs are not allowed anywhere in the permit area, and there is no dispersed camping between FR 7601 and Icicle Creek. Day use needs only a free self-issued wilderness permit. Because the quota season starts on 15 May, an early-spring ascent — when this couloir is normally in its best condition — falls outside the overnight permit requirement.
bivy.notes: The base camp for the route, about 4-4.5 mi and 2,200 ft from the Stuart Lake trailhead. Parties heading for the couloir generally camp toward the far, south end of the lake so they are already at the moraine in the morning; a large flat boulder there is a well-used pitch. In cold conditions, camping back in the trees off the shore is warmer and far more sheltered than the open lakeside. Typical starts from camp run between about 3 and 5 a.m., which puts you at the base of the couloir in the couple of hours before the sun reaches it.

bivy.name: Lake Constance
bivy.water: The lake itself — clear, cold and holding trout. It is the only water at camp, and there is none on the climb above.
bivy.capacity: A quota area with a small number of sites; parties describe pitching at the north end of the lake. Demand far exceeds supply.
bivy.permit: An Olympic National Park wilderness camping permit is required and Lake Constance is a designated quota area, so a reservation through Recreation.gov effectively has to be secured the morning the window opens — one party booked at 7 a.m. on the March release date for an August weekend. Fees are charged per person per night plus a reservation fee. Bear canisters are required. Campfires are prohibited (the lake is above the 3,500 ft fire closure elevation). There is a composting toilet at the lake; elsewhere solid waste is buried well away from camp and water and toilet paper is packed out.
bivy.notes: The only practical camp for the route and a brutal one to reach: an unmaintained climbers' path gaining roughly 3,200 ft in about 1.8 mi from the Dosewallips, steep enough that you are pulling on roots and logs, and that is after walking or biking several miles of the road washed out since 2002. Parties climb Constance from here and come back to the same camp the same day rather than moving a camp higher — there is no established upper camp on this side, and the ground above through Avalanche Canyon and the traverses is not somewhere you want to be carrying overnight loads.
